planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil; the low, flat-topped habit works best as a mass planting or foundation skirt rather than a specimen that needs vertical presence.

directions: This patented Monrovia selection, marketed as Emerald Spreader, grows as a dense, flat-topped mound considerably wider than it is tall, holding tightly packed, glossy dark-green needles even in the deep shade that stalls most other conifers. Its low horizontal branching makes it a strong substitute for broadleaf foundation shrubs under eaves or north-facing walls where little direct light ever reaches the soil. Shear lightly in late spring if a firmer mounded line is wanted, though the natural habit stays tidy with no pruning at all. As with every yew, the seed-bearing aril flesh is the only non-toxic part of the plant, and foliage should be kept well away from grazing livestock and curious pets.

planting.note: Site where the horizontal tiers of branching have room to widen for decades without crowding; underplant with low shade perennials rather than placing near walkways that would require cutting back the pendulous branchlets.

directions: Named for John Dovaston, who found this seedling near Westfelton, Shropshire, in the early 1800s, the cultivar grows a single leader with strictly horizontal main branches that cascade pendulous side-branchlets, giving mature specimens a layered, almost pagoda-like silhouette unlike any other yew form. Because the character depends on grafted or cutting-grown material staying true to the tiered branching pattern, seedlings from its fruit revert to an ordinary upright yew and are not used in the trade. It tolerates the same deep, dry shade that limits most conifers and needs little pruning beyond removing the occasional upright reversion shoot to preserve the tiered outline. Give it generous lateral room from the start, since the wide-spreading tiers are the entire point of growing this historic selection.

planting.note: Use as a low spreading groundcover or bank cover in dappled shade; a little more light than full shade keeps the seasonal gold tipping more pronounced through summer.

directions: A golden-needled sport of the wide-spreading cultivar 'Repandens', this low, horizontally branching yew pushes creamy-yellow new growth each season that gradually fades to green-gold and then dark green by the following year, giving a layered two-tone effect across the mound. It shares the parent's trailing habit and tolerance for heavy shade, dry soil, and root competition from nearby trees, but develops its brightest color with at least some filtered or morning sun rather than deepest shade. Left unpruned it forms a dense, slowly widening skirt useful on slopes or at the base of taller shrubs; occasional tip pruning encourages fresh gold growth rather than letting the plant settle into all-green foliage. Like all yews it bears red, fleshy, non-toxic arils around a single toxic seed, so plant away from areas grazed by livestock.

planting.note: Space to allow the naturally globe-shaped habit to fill in without crowding; works well as a sheared or unsheared hedge line along shaded foundations and property borders.

directions: This male hybrid yew forms a naturally dense, rounded globe of dark-green needles with little of the leggy, open growth that many yews show when left unpruned, making it one of the more reliably tidy choices for a foundation hedge in heavy shade. Because it is a male clone it never sets the fleshy red arils typical of female yews, which some gardeners prefer where the fallen fruit would otherwise be a litter or child-safety concern. It takes shearing into a tighter formal hedge as readily as it holds its loose globe shape left alone, and tolerates the dry, rooty shade under mature trees better than almost any other evergreen hedge plant. Avoid wet, poorly drained sites, since root rot rather than shade is the main threat to establishing yews of this type.

planting.note: Give young plants enough lateral room to develop their broad pyramidal shape; this is the most tree-like of the shade-tolerant yew forms and can eventually need more space than most foundation yews.

directions: Selected for a naturally broad, pyramidal outline with a single dominant leader, this Japanese yew form grows more tree-like over time than the mounding or spreading cultivars sold for small foundation spaces, and nurseries have long favored it as reliable, true-to-type seed-grown stock. Its dense, upright branching and dark needle color make it useful as an informal screen, windbreak, or large accent in partly shaded woodland-edge gardens where a true conifer silhouette is wanted but full sun is unavailable. It accepts shearing into a tighter cone shape for a more formal look, though left alone it keeps a naturally pleasing pyramidal form without corrective pruning. Like other yews it survives well in dry shade and compacted soil but struggles in sites that stay wet through winter.

planting.note: Plant where the unusually short, blunt needles can be appreciated up close, such as a shaded border edge or collector conifer bed, rather than massed as anonymous hedging.

directions: One of the oldest named English yew selections still in cultivation, this cultivar is immediately distinct from typical yews because of its short, blunt, closely spaced needles pressed tightly against the stems, giving the foliage a dense, almost box-like texture rather than the usual flat yew spray. Its slow, compact growth and male flowering habit make it a long-lived, low-maintenance choice for shaded borders where a fine, unusual texture is wanted among broader-leaved shade shrubs. It takes decades to reach significant size, so it suits small gardens and collector plantings better than large-scale screening. Culture is the same as other English yews: well-drained soil, tolerance of deep shade and dry root zones, and avoidance of waterlogged sites.

planting.note: Allow generous lateral space from the start, since this is one of the widest-spreading hybrid yews sold and resents being crowded or repeatedly sheared back to fit a tight foundation bed.

directions: This male hybrid yew builds a broad, flat-topped mound with strongly horizontal branching, reaching a much greater spread than height and making it one of the better choices for covering a wide shaded area without the plant ever growing tall enough to block a window or sightline. Its dense, dark-green needle coverage holds up well under the dry, low-light conditions beneath large shade trees where thinner-foliaged shrubs struggle. Because it is male it produces no fruit, which keeps the ground beneath it free of the sticky fallen arils that female yews drop in late summer. Light shearing can tighten the outline for a more formal look, but the plant's naturally wide, tiered silhouette is usually left unpruned in woodland-edge or foundation plantings.

planting.note: Site in a sheltered, partly shaded spot such as a courtyard or understory bed; the cream-striped needles scorch in hot, full sun exposure more readily than the plain green species.

directions: A slow-growing variegated sport of the common Japanese podocarpus, this cultivar carries irregular cream-to-white streaking down the length of each narrow, strap-like needle, giving an upright shrub a lighter, speckled appearance compared with the solid dark green of the species. Its naturally dense, upright branching and slow growth rate make it well suited to a shaded courtyard accent or large container where the unusual foliage color can be viewed at close range. It shares the species' tolerance for shade and pruning into clipped forms, though variegated growth is generally slower and less vigorous than reverted all-green shoots, which should be removed if they appear. Protect from hard freezes, since it has less cold tolerance than the plain green form and is best suited to mild, humid climates.
